title: Animated pixel-art vehicle icons
creator: Matthias_Oel
prompt: Create one original animated pixel-art icon as a Framer code component. Do not build a page, section, card, background, or reusable icon library. Before building, ask exactly two questions one after another using Framer’s multiple-choice question UI. First ask what the icon should show and provide several examples plus a custom-answer option. Second ask how the icon should animate continuously; base the suggested answers on the chosen subject and include a custom-answer option. After the second answer, immediately create the icon and do not ask about style, colors, size, layout, or technical implementation. Always use the same professional minimalist pixel-art direction: a clean and recognizable silhouette, balanced proportions, consistent pixel thickness, precise outlines, subtle pixel shading, and a polished appearance. Keep symmetrical subjects properly symmetrical and avoid messy, uneven, blurry, overly cute, or cartoon-like results unless explicitly requested. Choose a compact palette of approximately 3–6 colors that naturally fits the selected icon. Prioritize colors mentioned by the user, then colors from an uploaded reference, and otherwise choose an appropriate palette for the subject. Never force the same colors onto every icon. Uploaded images may guide the subject, proportions, palette, and animation idea, but never directly copy or trace protected artwork, logos, branding, code, or distinctive visual details. Draw the icon with Canvas on a logical pixel grid between 24×24 and 48×48 pixels. Use only integer coordinates and integer pixel sizes, disable image smoothing, use pixelated CSS rendering, support devicePixelRatio correctly, and keep the background transparent. Study the selected subject and design a continuous animation that communicates what the object naturally does. Animate meaningful internal parts and supporting details instead of simply scaling, rotating, or moving the entire icon. Keep the main icon visually anchored unless movement is natural for the subject or specifically requested. Never add generic floating, bouncing, or constant up-and-down movement by default. Combine one clear primary action with one or two restrained secondary details, such as moving parts, signals, sparks, particles, light pulses, wheels, flames, scan lines, or status changes. Structure the motion with a short resting phase, action phase, and smooth recovery so the loop remains easy to understand. Make the first and final animation states match perfectly and avoid abrupt resets, jumps, or disappearing pixels. Keep every possible animation state inside the component bounds. Calculate the frame from the combined bounds of all states, add only around 2–3 logical pixels of safety padding, and keep the icon optically centered throughout the animation. Use Framer auto-sizing with @framerSupportedLayoutWidth auto and @framerSupportedLayoutHeight auto so the component frame stays tightly wrapped around the icon. Do not create a full-width frame, oversized wrapper, invisible empty area, or unnecessary padding. Add Framer property controls for display size, primary color, outline color, accent color, animation speed, and animation intensity. Use sensible defaults based on the generated icon. Run the animation through one requestAnimationFrame loop using elapsed time. Store changing values in refs and never update React state on every frame. Do not use setInterval, resize the Canvas during the animation loop, or generate random values inside the loop. Precompute particles and reusable coordinates, keep their paths deterministic, and only update Canvas resolution when the component size or devicePixelRatio changes. Cancel requestAnimationFrame correctly when the component unmounts. Before finishing, verify the icon at multiple sizes and repeatedly test the continuous loop. The final result must be crisp, stable, balanced, smoothly animated, tightly framed, and completely free of flicker, clipping, blur, shaking, accidental gaps, uneven pixels, layout jumps, or visible animation resets.

title: GE90 turbofan engine cutaway
creator: anyapi_ai
prompt:
GE90-115B turbofan engine cutaway — the monster that powers the Boeing 777. Single HTML file.

FRONT FAN (left): massive 3.25m diameter fan with 22 curved composite blades. Fan spinning at 2500 RPM. Air splits — blue cold bypass air rushes around the outside (80% of thrust), hot core air enters compressor.

COMPRESSOR: 10-stage high-pressure compressor. Each stage of blades gets smaller, compressing air. Blue air progressively turning orange/red as it heats and compresses.

COMBUSTOR: annular combustion chamber. Fuel injectors spraying kerosene, bright orange-white flame ring. Temperature jumps to 1500°C. Combustion glow pulsing.

TURBINE: 2-stage high-pressure turbine driving compressor, 6-stage low-pressure turbine driving fan. Blades glowing red-hot, spinning opposite directions. HOT exhaust (orange-red gas) blasting out rear through exhaust nozzle.

CHEVRON NOZZLE: serrated trailing edge at exhaust, mixing hot jet with cold bypass air — noise reduction. Visible exhaust plume with mach diamonds.

EXTERNAL: nacelle cowling, thrust reverser cascade vanes visible, engine pylon mounting to wing stub.

ANIMATION: fan spin, compressor stages at increasing speeds, fuel spray flicker, combustion pulse, turbine spin, bypass air smooth flow, exhaust pulsing, thrust reverser stow/deploy hint.

COLORS: titanium fan silver, hot section glow orange-to-white, bypass air ice blue, exhaust dark orange, nacelle white/grey. Dark technical background. Labels: Fan, Compressor, Combustor, Turbine, Exhaust.
